Every time I match with women on dating apps, I end up putting in all the work, from trying to get to know them, propose interesting dates to just getting the conversation started and keep it going. I don’t know why, and frankly, I’m getting tired of it.

It doesn’t matter which app I’m on, Hinge, Bumble, OKC, whatever: I match with someone, I put in a lot of work to try to connect with them and if I get more than one word replies it’s a goddamn miracle. On those oh so rare days when it DOES happen, they put absolutely no effort into trying to get to know me in return.

I have tried almost everything to change things up. I try to be funny and playful. I try to lead with deeper topics. I mention things specifically in their profile and ask questions so they know I actually read it. I’ve used obviously cheesy pick-up lines, even tried sending gifs on the apps that allow it. I’ve double-texted, I’ve single-texted, I’ve sent “are you still there?” messages and I’ve sent one message and waited for a response. Crickets. Silence. One word replies.

This makes no sense to me, especially when Ive matched with women who say that they want to skip the small talk, get deep and have real, meaningful conversations. OK, well, I sent them real, deep and meaningful questions based off things that they say they’re into in their profiles and maybe I will get a thumbs up or smiley face response before days of silence and eventually getting unmatched.

For the record, I’ve put effort into my profile. My pics are good and varied, I answer a variety of prompts including doing voice prompts or video responses, I try to show my personality and I know I’m a decent looking guy with a life and hobbies. I guess I just don’t understand why someone would match with me and then just never put in even the slightest effort to actually connect with someone who’s trying to do exactly what they say they want.
It’s hard not to take this personally and it’s getting harder not to think that all the bros who talk about women competing for the same 10% of men are right.
What’s the deal with this?
Tired Of The App Silent Treatment

You’re certainly not alone in this; there are dozens upon dozens of posts from men with similar complaints on myriad dating and dating app subreddits alone – many within a few days of writing this. The thing that their – and your – complaints all have in common is that they all run into the problem that is that this is fundamentally an unanswerable question. It’s unanswerable because there’s a flaw baked into the premise: that this is a problem that is universal behavior from women or that it’s gendered in the first place.

That is: this isn’t an “all women” thing, or even a “women” thing. It’s a dating app problem, not something having to do with the gender of the people involved. It just feels that way because you’re trying to match with women, rather than trying to match with men. If you were trying to match with men – especially as a woman – then you would have a very similar experience: first messages that average less than 12 characters – not words, characters, including spaces and punctuation – and people unmatching shortly afterwards.

Now for the sake of argument, TOAST, let’s assume that your profile is top notch, your photos are great and your messages are thoughtful, individually crafted and sincere – all things that many men on dating apps tend to have a problem with. We will also assume that you’re matching with people who are compatible with you – a thing that’s very hard to gauge from a Hinge or Tinder profile, no matter how thoroughly filled out.
So, ruling out the classic “skill issue” and incompatible matches, what’s left? Why is this a recurring issue for you?

Well, because at the end of the day, it’s a platform issue, something that’s baked into the apps themselves.
While men and women run into similar issues, it tends to be coming from different places, and both help exacerbate the problem. In fact, one tends to contribute directly towards the other. The difference is that one group’s frustration comes from folks who are going as low-effort as possible; the other is the response to those low-investment efforts.

Let’s start with something obvious: men and women have a tendency to use the apps in ways that are entirely at cross-purposes. The point of the apps is – in theory – to make meeting people easier, more efficient, less stressful and anxiety-provoking. All well and good. But making things “more efficient” tacitly encourages greater efforts at finding ways to make it even more efficient, including “putting in less effort in order to increase the number of shots you take” – which includes obvious copy-pasted messages, employing LLMs to act as a digital Cyrano and swiping right on everyone.

blocks.x: I’ve talked before about the ways that men use the apps and the “strategy” of swiping right on everyone in hopes of maximizing the matches they get (or, depending on who you ask “are ‘forced’ into swiping right to get any matches”) and why it’s incredibly counterproductive. It’s the shotgun approach to dating distilled down to its essence: throw as much lead out as possible and you’ll connect with something. On dating apps, it supposedly serves a double purpose: not only maximizing matches for matches sake, but improving one’s algorithm rating by increasing the number of matches, responses and engagement rates.

But the problem is that these attempts at maximizing efficiency works against the very goals they’re trying to achieve. Leaving aside the attempts to game the algorithm, the majority of men on the apps are aren’t trying to find a date, they’re trying to find someone willing to fuck while expending as little effort in the search as they possibly can. This is why almost every woman with a dating app profile has dozens of stories of matching with guys whose first or second message is entirely about sending nudes or trying to get them to come over and bang.
Now put a pin in that, we’ll be coming back to it.
Now, we’re going to flip to the other side of the equation and what is the typical experience for women on the apps and why there’s often what seems to be little “effort” being expended by women.

See one of the things that gets lost in all the procto-numerology of “80%-90% of women are competing for 10% of the men” is the far more important ratio: the percentage of male users to female users on the apps. In most cases, women are vastly outnumbered by men on the apps, regardless of platform or brand. Tinder, Hinge, OKCupid, Match, eHarmony, Bumble, Coffee Meets Bagel, Farmers Only, Christian Mingle, The League, Raya… in virtually every case, the ratio of men to women tends to be close to 3:1 on average. While there’s a little wiggle-room depending on the specific platform, there are simply far more men using dating apps than women. This means that, by virtue of the demographics involved, women are going to be getting far more attention from men than men will from women. This is not a judgement; it’s just numbers.

However, this gets exacerbated by the fact that society’s gender dynamics follow us everywhere, including online. And in this case, the relevant issue that men are more likely to make the first move than women are. There’re a number of reasons for this, but most of it comes down to socialization: men are encouraged to make the first move, women are taught not to and are in fact, often punished for doing so.

This is an issue that has even affected apps that were explicitly designed to change things up; even Bumble has chosen to scrap its “women make the first move” setup in exchange for a more traditional “anyone can start the conversation”. This has the net effect of women being inundated with matches and messages from men… many of which are low effort at best.

Despite how this often sounds to men – consider how many men talk about how they’d love to get the same sort of attention from women that women complain about from men – this actually works against the goal of meeting people easily and efficiently. Even if we grant that all the profiles and messages are all high-quality and sincere effort… that still leaves women in the position of the dating app equivalent of trying to drink from the firehose.

People in general, all across the gender spectrum, have only so much mental bandwidth to apply to tasks, and that includes managing various conversations or interactions with people. Consider the cognitive strain of trying to maintain just two or three conversations with people you know on WhatsApp simultaneously. Now consider trying to maintain those conversations while also, say, trying to complete that spreadsheet your manager wants finished by the end of business.
And now consider all of that, except those conversations are with relative strangers. Strangers who want to get into your pants.

The fact of the matter is that most people are going to get worn out just trying to juggle multiple conversations with friends, people they know, love and are close to. It’s even harder when you’re dealing with strangers and trying to suss out whether there’s any chemistry there, catch a vibe and decide if you like them well enough and feel safe enough to risk meeting them in person.
And it’s harder still when you’re getting notifications from more and more people, even as you’re trying to manage those conversations.

That alone means that many conversations and matches are just going to go nowhere. It has nothing to do with the quality of the message or the profile of the person sending the message, but of the effort it requires on the part of the person receiving them. Nobody, no matter how well-intentioned or willing to give folks a chance, has infinite mental bandwidth or attention to give. At some point, they’re going to max out, and that means that something is going to give. They are going to hit a point where they simply cannot give the same level of attention or consideration to every message that comes in, especially if they’re actively engaged in a conversation with someone already.

That means that matches and messages that come later tend to get ignored, or the person resolves to respond to them later. Many times, that “like” or smile emoji you’re getting back isn’t a brush-off, it’s an acknowledgement – a placeholder that says “hey, wanted you to know I saw this, even if I can’t reply or don’t have anything to say right this instant”.

That doesn’t mean that you’re getting ignored or passed over because you’re not one of the mythic (and imaginary) 10 – 20%. It means that through a quirk of timing and bad luck, you weren’t the first message they saw or responded to. You’re in the queue, but there’s no real way to say when or even if the person will get to you.
https://s3-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/widget-images/become-patron-widget-medium%402x.png

Which sucks, sure, but you can’t really do anything about it or control for it. It’s baked into the system; you can’t ensure that you’re going to catch a stranger on the apps at a time when they’ll be receptive to getting a message from you. Nobody can.

This is why dating, especially on the apps, is a numbers game; you can’t guarantee that you’re sending your perfect message at the perfect time. You can only send out that ping and hope you get a response. Watching that read receipt and looking for the three dots like Gatsby watching the green lights in the bay just exacerbates your frustration; the only thing you can do is fire and forget, while trusting that the app will let you know if and when they respond.

(I would also point out that the apps’ own patterns encourage mindless swiping, while also pushing you to pay more for algorithmic boosts in the form of higher subscription tiers or one-off tools like roses or temporary high visibility… but that’s a separate rant entirely.)

But the math changes even further when – returning to what I said earlier – many if not most of those matches from men are low-effort attempts from people employing the shotgun technique. For women on the receiving end of the shotgun approach, many of the matches they get are from people who never intended to match with them in the first place. The men who swiped right on them just wanted to maximize their matches and will sort out which women they actually want to talk to afterwards.

So, now you have women who are trying to match with people in good faith only to find out that the person trying to match with them was really just trying to game the algorithm and increase their internal profile score, while many more were just looking for the lowest-effort blowjob they could find.

The apps can be frustrating and exhausting enough when you’re getting deluged with genuine attention. When the attention someone is getting is impersonal at best or even just as a means of trying to shown in the feeds of the folks they actually want to match with… well, now you have a recipe for exasperation and discouragement, which leads to people closing their accounts entirely. So sometimes the reason why you get that thumbs up or smiley face before getting unmatched isn’t because they decided to go with a different candidate, but because they dipped out entirely before they ever got around to responding to you.
Which, again, absolutely sucks. But it’s not a judgement on you, your desirability or your worth as a person. It’s, again, bad luck and bad timing, things that you simply cannot control for.

Now, here’s the other thing to consider: if you’re in a position where it’s not bad timing and you do have that person’s full attention and you’re either getting low-effort replies or responses from someone who’s showing no reciprocal effort to get to know you, you can always unmatch them, yourself. And frankly, you should, rather than investing time and energy in someone who seems to show no interest in investing in you.

I fully understand wanting to make things work, especially if you have been feeling frustrated or not getting matches, but there’s no benefit to straining your back by trying to carry on the entire conversation. The level of effort it takes to change that dynamic is never going to be commensurate with the results; the odds are high that it’s simply not going to lead to a date, and if it does, it’s not going to be a date that leads to another. So, instead of falling into a sunk-cost fallacy, it’s better to unmatch and focus on someone who is showing mutual interest instead.

Yes, depending on your situation, that may mean that it will be a while before you get another match who is showing mutual interest in getting to know you. But this is precisely why I say that dating apps should be a supplement to meeting people, not a replacement. You’ll have far better results – as well as a better use of your time and energy and just having a better time overall – to go out, be social and do things that you enjoy with other people. You’ll have far more fun, spend time with friends old and new… and quite possibly meet someone special who’s looking for someone just like you.

That’s going to be a far better use of your limited time on this Earth than trying to persist through the conversational equivalent of pulling teeth… and it’s far more likely to lead to something great.
Good luck.
Hi Doc!
I’m currently having a bit of an internal debate that I’d like your two cents on.

I met a man, we’ll call him Trevor, on Hinge a few weeks ago. We set up a first date almost IMMEDIATELY. Not that I’m complaining; no one involved is getting any younger. We went out for dinner and I paid. Only fair as I was the one who asked him out.
https://www.doctornerdlove.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/shutterstock_1721152858.jpg

Over the course of our first two dates, I discovered that Trevor checks A LOT of my boxes. We’re both big on communication. We had the conversation about monogamy vs. non-monogamy, and we seem to be on the same page about that. He’s looking to date with intention, which is refreshing to hear. I’m at the point in my life where I’m done with the hookups and one-night stands and casual sex. That was for my 20s and even then, I was never looking for JUST sex. Also, he’s a spooky bitch like me.
However, I’m realizing that I’m just not attracted to him. I mean, I wouldn’t kick him out of bed but I don’t look at him and say “My god, I must have you now.”
I see a relationship with him and it would be a healthy one. I feel as if I’d be doing myself a disservice by whittling this down to something as superficial as physical attraction.
I’d love to hear your take on this.
Sincerely,
Witty Sign-Off

Just to make sure that I’m understanding you: it’s not that Trevor is unattractive or ugly. As you say, you wouldn’t kick him out of bed, which suggests to me that he isn’t unappealing or a turn-off, so much as he’s not the kind of hot that makes your clothes spontaneously explode off of you.

You also say that you’re done with hookups, casual sex and one-night stands. So, would I be correct in thinking that the kind of men you were meeting for those hookups were the “OMG Take Me Now” hot? And – seeing as those no longer hold interest for you – the hotties were lacking qualities besides their looks?

Assuming that I’m not off base, it sounds like up until now you’ve been prioritizing for a specific kind of attractiveness for a specific kind of connection. Now that those particular kinds of encounters don’t do it for you, it makes sense to me that maybe it’s time to prioritize other aspects in the people you date.

Here’s the thing: relationships and attraction tend to be about the holistic person, not just looks. While looks can be great for initial and short-term sexual attraction, there’s a very strong fall-off over time in the importance of conventional attractiveness. Humans are infinitely adaptable after all, and we can get used to damn near anything… including someone who’s stupidly, blisteringly hot. As the infamous quote goes: they can be the hottest actress in the world, but after a while, it’s like fucking the couch”. That is: the effects of conventional hotness are directly correlated with their novelty; as we get accustomed to being with that person, the impact of their looks alone diminishes over time. It’s not that they’ve become ugly; it’s that we’ve gotten used to them and now they’re not Studly Goodnight, they’re Ken. The dude who you’ve seen fart, scratch his balls, pick his nose, wake up from the couch after drooling on himself while rocking some truly epic bed-head and matching designer bags under his eyes.

However, the impact of things like attentiveness, consideration, kindness and affection tend to last. So does the value of just enjoying their company; being fun to spend time with tends to top the list of traits that encourage and support long-term relationships.

And just as importantly, the longer you know someone – especially when you enjoy their company – the more they tend to grow on you and the more you tend to appreciate the things that make them unique. So while Chad Thundercock may make a hell of a first impression, Johnny’s smile with the slightly crooked tooth often ends up being the thing that your mind keeps coming back to that makes you smile in turn.

Right now, you’ve had two dates with Trevor and from the sound of it, they went swimmingly. You two are in alignment on many, if not most of the things you want in a relationship, and he has qualities that were apparently lacking in your hookup partners. I think you could do far worse than to keep seeing him and see what develops. You don’t need to commit to anything more than just continuing to see him; you certainly shouldn’t agree to something long-term when you’re still thinking things through. But I think it could be worth your time to see if you’re not attracted to him at all, or if the attraction to him is different than with the guys you were seeing before. Different, after all, is not the same as “better” vs “worse, nor “hotter” vs “not”. Sometimes different translates to “wait, why haven’t I been looking for this before?”

If it’s truly the case that you don’t find him attractive – as opposed to “he’s not AS hot as my casual partners” – then hey, you’ve given it an honest try. In that case, you’re able to move on, knowing that you won’t be kicking yourself down the line for not giving him a chance.
But you might be surprised to find out that your tastes and priorities have changed, just as the relationships you want have changed. But there’s really only one way to find out.
Good luck.

I fully understand wanting to make things work, especially if you have been feeling frustrated or not getting matches, but there’s no benefit to straining your back by trying to carry on the entire conversation. The level of effort it takes to change that dynamic is never going to be commensurate with the results; the odds are high that it’s simply not going to lead to a date, and if it does, it’s not going to be a date that leads to another. So, instead of falling into a sunk-cost fallacy, it’s better to unmatch and focus on someone who is showing mutual interest instead.

Yes, depending on your situation, that may mean that it will be a while before you get another match who is showing mutual interest in getting to know you. But this is precisely why I say that dating apps should be a supplement to meeting people, not a replacement. You’ll have far better results – as well as a better use of your time and energy and just having a better time overall – to go out, be social and do things that you enjoy with other people. You’ll have far more fun, spend time with friends old and new… and quite possibly meet someone special who’s looking for someone just like you.

That’s going to be a far better use of your limited time on this Earth than trying to persist through the conversational equivalent of pulling teeth… and it’s far more likely to lead to something great.

Good luck.

Witty Sign-Off

Just to make sure that I’m understanding you: it’s not that Trevor is unattractive or ugly. As you say, you wouldn’t kick him out of bed, which suggests to me that he isn’t unappealing or a turn-off, so much as he’s not the kind of hot that makes your clothes spontaneously explode off of you.

You also say that you’re done with hookups, casual sex and one-night stands. So, would I be correct in thinking that the kind of men you were meeting for those hookups were the “OMG Take Me Now” hot? And – seeing as those no longer hold interest for you – the hotties were lacking qualities besides their looks?

Assuming that I’m not off base, it sounds like up until now you’ve been prioritizing for a specific kind of attractiveness for a specific kind of connection. Now that those particular kinds of encounters don’t do it for you, it makes sense to me that maybe it’s time to prioritize other aspects in the people you date.

Here’s the thing: relationships and attraction tend to be about the holistic person, not just looks. While looks can be great for initial and short-term sexual attraction, there’s a very strong fall-off over time in the importance of conventional attractiveness. Humans are infinitely adaptable after all, and we can get used to damn near anything… including someone who’s stupidly, blisteringly hot. As the infamous quote goes: they can be the hottest actress in the world, but after a while, it’s like fucking the couch”. That is: the effects of conventional hotness are directly correlated with their novelty; as we get accustomed to being with that person, the impact of their looks alone diminishes over time. It’s not that they’ve become ugly; it’s that we’ve gotten used to them and now they’re not Studly Goodnight, they’re Ken. The dude who you’ve seen fart, scratch his balls, pick his nose, wake up from the couch after drooling on himself while rocking some truly epic bed-head and matching designer bags under his eyes.

However, the impact of things like attentiveness, consideration, kindness and affection tend to last. So does the value of just enjoying their company; being fun to spend time with tends to top the list of traits that encourage and support long-term relationships.

And just as importantly, the longer you know someone – especially when you enjoy their company – the more they tend to grow on you and the more you tend to appreciate the things that make them unique. So while Chad Thundercock may make a hell of a first impression, Johnny’s smile with the slightly crooked tooth often ends up being the thing that your mind keeps coming back to that makes you smile in turn.

Right now, you’ve had two dates with Trevor and from the sound of it, they went swimmingly. You two are in alignment on many, if not most of the things you want in a relationship, and he has qualities that were apparently lacking in your hookup partners. I think you could do far worse than to keep seeing him and see what develops. You don’t need to commit to anything more than just continuing to see him; you certainly shouldn’t agree to something long-term when you’re still thinking things through. But I think it could be worth your time to see if you’re not attracted to him at all, or if the attraction to him is different than with the guys you were seeing before. Different, after all, is not the same as “better” vs “worse, nor “hotter” vs “not”. Sometimes different translates to “wait, why haven’t I been looking for this before?”

If it’s truly the case that you don’t find him attractive – as opposed to “he’s not AS hot as my casual partners” – then hey, you’ve given it an honest try. In that case, you’re able to move on, knowing that you won’t be kicking yourself down the line for not giving him a chance.
But you might be surprised to find out that your tastes and priorities have changed, just as the relationships you want have changed. But there’s really only one way to find out.

Good luck.
